prompt.context: Our client is the health minister of a small country. The country is small and on the upper end of the GDP spectrum for countries of its size. The country's health system is completely free to its citizens and is funded by taxpayer money. Patients can visit one of 30 clinics spread throughout the country for a primary care visit, and then get referred to one of 2 larger hospitals if more intensive procedures are required. There are a few private systems for the richest citizens, but they are so small in comparison to the public system that they won't be considered at all in our study. The GDP, and thus the tax returns for the country, have been growing at a 5% rate. However, the healthcare budget has required 10% growth to keep up with demand. The health minister is concerned that at this rate the healthcare system will become unsustainable.
prompt.question: The health minister has hired us to figure out why the healthcare budget is requiring this level of growth and what can be done to reduce it.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current population of the country?
Is the population expected to change over the next 10 years?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the census estimates the population will grow by 30% over the next 10 years, reaching 1.3 million.

clarifying_info.q: How many visits does the average citizen make per year, and at what cost?
clarifying_info.a: The average citizen goes through the healthcare system 5 times a year at an average cost of $50 per visit.

clarifying_info.q: What is the proposed copayment amount?
clarifying_info.a: The health minister is considering a $5 per visit copayment covering all individual visits regardless of specialty.

clarifying_info.q: How would the copayment affect visit frequency?
clarifying_info.a: Estimates suggest visits would decrease from 5 to 4.5 per citizen per year.

exhibits.title: Population Demographics and Healthcare Cost by Age Group
exhibits.shows: A table showing the percentage of population today and in 10 years for three age cohorts (0-21, 22-65, 65+), along with the average healthcare cost per person per year for each cohort.

columns: Average HC cost per person per year

framework: Demand-side drivers: demographic changes (aging population, population growth) increasing the number and costliness of patients
Demand-side drivers: changes in health perception or awareness causing citizens to seek care more frequently
Demand-side drivers: incentive structures of doctors and hospitals encouraging more visits or unnecessary referrals to the 2 larger hospitals
Supply-side drivers: shortage of doctors or resources bidding up prices for the same services
Supply-side drivers: lack of preventative care making patients less healthy and thus requiring more expensive care when they do fall ill

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — What factors are driving the healthcare budget growth?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose a structured framework covering both demand-side and supply-side drivers. Demand: demographic shifts (aging, population growth), changes in health-seeking behavior, physician/hospital incentive misalignment encouraging over-referral. Supply: resource/doctor shortages driving up prices, insufficient preventative care leading to higher downstream costs.

questions.prompt: Phase 2a — Looking at the demographic table (Exhibit 1), what do you observe?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the population is aging: the 65+ cohort doubles from 10% to 20%, while the 0-21 cohort halves from 20% to 10%. Since the 65+ cohort costs $4,000 per person vs. $1,000 for the youngest cohort, this redistribution will substantially increase average per-capita healthcare cost. The 22-65 cohort stays constant at 70%. The candidate should conclude that healthcare spending will increase at an even greater rate than the current 10%, worsening the minister's problem.

questions.prompt: Phase 2b — Calculate current total healthcare spending and projected spending in 10 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute a weighted average cost per citizen today and in 10 years, then multiply by the appropriate population. The candidate must ask about (or be guided toward) the 30% population growth to arrive at 1.3M future citizens. React to the magnitude of the percent increase.

math.setup: Current: weighted average cost per citizen × 1M population. Future: weighted average cost per citizen (new distribution) × 1.3M population.
steps: Acceptable rounding: if $950M rounded to $1B, percent increase ≈ 62.5%, equally significant
math.answer: Current spending ≈ $950M; projected spending in 10 years ≈ $1.625B; approximately a 71% increase.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — The health minister is considering a $5 per visit copayment. What would be the financial impact?
questions.guidance: Candidate should reason that: (1) the out-of-pocket cost to the system per visit drops from $50 to $45 because the citizen pays $5; (2) visits per citizen will decrease from 5 to 4.5 because care is no longer fully free. Candidate must then calculate the total current cost of routine visits, total cost under the plan, and the savings — both in absolute terms and as a percentage of total healthcare spending ($950M).

math.setup: Compare total visit cost under current system vs. under copayment plan using 1M citizens.
steps: Current total visit cost: 5 visits × $50 per visit × 1,000,000 citizens = $250M
Future total visit cost: 4.5 visits × $45 per visit × 1,000,000 citizens = $202.5M
Reduction as share of total healthcare budget: $50M / $950M ≈ 5%
math.answer: The copayment saves approximately $50M, reducing routine visit costs by ~20% and total healthcare spending by ~5%.

brainstorming.prompt: The copayment seems financially helpful. What are the risks of the copayment, and what alternative or complementary measures could the minister consider?

categories.name: Copayment Risks
ideas: Equity / access for the poorest citizens who may not be able to afford even a $5 copay — consider a sliding scale based on per-capita income
Political backlash — the public may react negatively to any charge for previously free care, creating repercussions for the minister's party; a survey could gauge public sentiment
Insufficient deterrence — $5 may not deter patients who abuse the system with superfluous visits; a sliding scale based on visit acuity or type could be more effective
Emergency care barrier — the copayment could delay people seeking care in emergencies; fee waiver for emergency situations should be considered

categories.name: Alternative / Complementary Measures
ideas: Transparency — publish the cost of treatments so physicians factor cost into prescribing decisions
Quotas and rules — require a minimum share of generic drug prescriptions rather than branded drugs; mandate outpatient procedures when clinically appropriate instead of inpatient stays
Limiting visit types — regulate visits that only need to occur once a year (e.g., routine eye exams) to prevent overuse
Investing in preventative care — healthier citizens require less acute care; focusing resources on preventative programs can reduce long-run spending

recommendation: We estimate healthcare spending will increase approximately 70% over the next 10 years, driven by two factors: a 30% population increase and a significant demographic aging (the 65+ cohort doubling from 10% to 20% of population).

The proposed $5 copayment is a good near-term starting point — it could reduce total healthcare costs by roughly 5% immediately — but must be designed carefully to avoid adverse effects on quality of care, access for lower-income citizens, and political feasibility.

From a long-term perspective the system's sustainability will require structural measures: visit-type regulations to prevent overuse of certain services, and increased investment in preventative care to reduce downstream acute-care demand.
risks: Copayment may be unaffordable for low-income citizens, creating inequitable access
Public opposition could make the policy politically untenable
A fixed $5 fee may be insufficient to deter truly superfluous visits
Without parallel supply-side reforms, demand reduction alone may not close the 10% annual budget growth gap
next_steps: Conduct a public survey to gauge political feasibility of the copayment
Design an income-based sliding scale to protect low-income citizens
Engage physicians in crafting prescribing rules (generics, outpatient preference) to ensure clinical buy-in
Commission a detailed analysis of preventative care investment options and their projected long-run savings
Monitor demographic trends and revisit the 10-year forecast annually
